rows.stem:
Arrange the following in the increasing order of the property mentioned :
(a) \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\), \(\mathrm{ClCH_2COOH}\), \(\mathrm{FCH_2COOH}\) (Acid strength)
(b) \(\mathrm{CH_3CHO}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_3}\) (Boiling Points)
rows.solution:
(a) Increasing acid strength:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH} < \mathrm{ClCH_2COOH} < \mathrm{FCH_2COOH}\)

Acid strength is decided by the stability of the carboxylate anion left behind, and anything WITHDRAWING electron density spreads the negative charge and stabilises it.

Acetic acid's METHYL group does the opposite, RELEASING density and intensifying the charge, so it is the weakest of the three. Both halogens withdraw, and FLUORINE — the more electronegative — withdraws more strongly than chlorine.

The \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) values record the order: 4.76, 2.86, 2.59.

(b) Increasing boiling point:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_3} < \mathrm{CH_3CHO} < \mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}\)

All three are of comparable molar mass — 44, 44 and 46 — so the order is set entirely by INTERMOLECULAR FORCES.

PROPANE is non-polar and has only weak dispersion forces, so it boils at 231 K. ETHANAL has a polar carbonyl group and so dipole-dipole attraction, but no \(\mathrm{O-H}\), so it boils at 293 K. ETHANOL has an \(\mathrm{O-H}\) group and forms HYDROGEN BONDS, much the strongest of these forces, so it boils at 351 K.

The gap between ethanal and ethanol is the measure of what a hydrogen bond is worth: nearly 60 degrees, for molecules of almost identical mass.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the IUPAC name of the following complex :
\(\mathrm{K_3[Cr(C_2O_4)_3]}\)
(b) On the basis of crystal field theory, write the electronic configuration of \(\mathrm{d^5}\) ion if \(\Delta_0 < \mathrm{P}\).
(c) What are ambidentate ligands ?
rows.solution:
(a) The complex is the ANION — three potassiums outside make it \(3-\) — so its name takes the \(-\mathrm{ATE}\) suffix. Three oxalate ligands give \(-6\) against that \(3-\), so chromium is \(+3\):
POTASSIUM TRIOXALATOCHROMATE(III)

The cation is named first and written as a separate word, exactly as in an ordinary salt. Note that the metal's stem here is simply "chromate"; some metals take a Latin-derived stem in an anionic complex, iron becoming "ferrate" and copper "cuprate".

(b) The configuration is \(t_{2g}^3\,e_g^2\).

An octahedral field splits the d orbitals into a lower set of three and an upper set of two, separated by \(\Delta_0\). Each electron chooses between promotion to the upper set, costing \(\Delta_0\), and pairing in the lower set, costing the pairing energy \(\mathrm{P}\).

With \(\Delta_0 < \mathrm{P}\) — a WEAK FIELD — promotion is the cheaper option, so the electrons spread out as widely as they can, one to each of the five orbitals. All FIVE are unpaired: a HIGH SPIN complex with the maximum possible moment, \(\mu = 5{\cdot}92\) B.M.

A strong field would have given \(t_{2g}^5\,e_g^0\) instead, with one unpaired electron and \(\mu = 1{\cdot}73\) B.M.

(c) AMBIDENTATE LIGANDS are ligands that have TWO DIFFERENT DONOR ATOMS and can bind the metal through EITHER of them — but only ONE AT A TIME, so they remain monodentate.

Examples: the NITRITE ion, binding through nitrogen as nitrito-N or through oxygen as nitrito-O; the THIOCYANATE ion, through nitrogen or sulphur; the CYANIDE ion, through carbon or nitrogen.

They are the cause of LINKAGE ISOMERISM. \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(NO_2)]^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(ONO)]^{2+}}\) contain the same atoms in the same numbers but differ in which atom is attached — and differ visibly, one being yellow and the other red.

Note the contrast with a BIDENTATE ligand, which also has two donor atoms but uses BOTH at once, closing a chelate ring.

rows.stem:
Observe the graph shown in figure and answer the following questions :
(a) What is the order of the reaction ?
(b) What is the slope of the curve?
(c) Write the relationship between \(k\) and \(t_{1/2}\) (half life period).
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the whole question is 'observe the graph shown in figure'; the stem names no data at all and the printed plot is the only source of it. The plot is DELIBERATELY NOT described here, because reading its axes IS the answer to sub-part (a). Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
The graph plots \(\log\left([\mathrm{R}]_0/[\mathrm{R}]\right)\) against TIME and gives a STRAIGHT LINE THROUGH THE ORIGIN.

(a) The reaction is FIRST ORDER.

The integrated first order rate law rearranges to exactly the form the graph shows:
\(\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]} = \dfrac{k}{2{\cdot}303}\,t\)

No other order gives a straight line for these axes — a zero order reaction gives one for \([\mathrm{R}]\) against \(t\), and a second order one for \(1/[\mathrm{R}]\) against \(t\). Which plot straightens is how the order is found from experimental data.

(b) The SLOPE is \(\dfrac{k}{2{\cdot}303}\).

Comparing with \(y = mx\), the coefficient of \(t\) is the slope, so measuring it gives the rate constant: \(k = 2{\cdot}303 \times \text{slope}\).

(c) The relationship between the rate constant and the half-life is
\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{k}\), that is \(k = \dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{t_{1/2}}\)

Note what is ABSENT from it: the initial concentration. For a first order reaction the half-life does not depend on how much material one starts with, which is why radioactive decay has a fixed half-life whatever the size of the sample.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Give reasons for the following statements :
(a) Transition elements and their compounds act as good catalysts.
(b) \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{(Mn^{2+}/Mn)}}\) value is highly negative as compared to other elements.
(c) \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) is a strong reducing agent.
rows.solution:
(a) Because of their VARIABLE OXIDATION STATES and their ability to form INTERMEDIATE compounds with the reactants.

A catalyst works by offering a path of LOWER ACTIVATION ENERGY, and a transition metal does this by accepting electrons from one reactant and passing them to another — changing oxidation state as it goes, then returning to its original state so that it is not consumed. Vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process cycles between \(+5\) and \(+4\) in just this way.

Finely divided transition metals also provide a large SURFACE on which reactant molecules are ADSORBED and held close together with their bonds weakened, as iron does in the Haber process.

(b) Because \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) has the exceptionally stable HALF-FILLED \(3d^5\) configuration.

Manganese is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^2\), so losing the two \(4s\) electrons gives an ion with every \(3d\) orbital singly occupied and all five spins parallel — an arrangement of unusual stability, with the electrons spread as widely as possible and the exchange energy at a maximum.

The metal therefore gives up those two electrons very readily, and a metal easily oxidised has a highly NEGATIVE reduction potential. At \(-1{\cdot}18\) V manganese is the most negative in the row.

Its unusually LOW enthalpy of atomisation contributes as well, making the metal cheap to break apart in the first place.

(c) Because \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) reaches a stable configuration by GIVING UP an electron.

Chromium(II) is \(3d^4\). Losing one more electron gives \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\), which is \(3d^3\) — in an octahedral aqueous environment the stable HALF-FILLED \(t_{2g}^3\) arrangement, with one electron in each of the three lower orbitals.

A species that gives up an electron readily IS a reducing agent, and chromium(II) does so eagerly: \(E^{\circ}\) for the couple is \(-0{\cdot}41\) V, negative enough that a chromium(II) solution reduces even water, liberating hydrogen.

rows.stem: An aromatic compound 'A' (\(\mathrm{C_7H_6O_2}\)) on reaction with aqueous ammonia and heating forms compound 'B'. 'B' on heating with \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) and alcoholic potash forms a compound 'C' of molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_6H_7N}\). Write the reactions involved and identify 'A', 'B', 'C'.
rows.solution:
The formula \(\mathrm{C_7H_6O_2}\), aromatic and with two oxygens, points to BENZOIC ACID.

Aqueous ammonia gives the ammonium salt, which loses water on heating to give the AMIDE:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\), benzoic acid
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{C_6H_5CONH_2}\), benzamide
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COOH} + \mathrm{NH_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5COONH_4} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{C_6H_5CONH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Bromine with alcoholic potash is the HOFMANN BROMAMIDE DEGRADATION, which converts an amide to a primary amine with ONE CARBON FEWER:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\), aniline
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CONH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{KOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} + \mathrm{K_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{KBr} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The CARBON COUNT is what confirms the last step: the formula \(\mathrm{C_6H_7N}\) has six carbons where the amide had seven, and losing exactly one is the signature of this reaction. The lost carbon is the carbonyl carbon, which leaves as carbonate, while the phenyl group migrates to the nitrogen.
